question: Should university be free?
for: Opens higher education to talented students from poor families
Society benefits from a more educated workforce
Graduates pay more tax over their working lives
against: Very expensive for governments
Taxpayers who did not go to university pay for those who did
May lead to overcrowded courses and lower quality
examples: Germany abolished tuition fees for public universities in 2014
Some countries offer free places only for subjects with skills shortages

question: Is technology making people less sociable?
for: People spend time on phones instead of talking face to face
Online friendships can be shallow
Children may have fewer chances to develop social skills
against: Technology helps people keep in touch over long distances
Online groups connect people with shared interests
Shy people may find it easier to start conversations online
examples: Video calls let families separated by migration see each other
Online communities support people with rare illnesses

question: Who is responsible for protecting the environment?
for: Governments can make laws and invest on a large scale
Companies produce most emissions and waste
Individual actions are small compared with industry
against: Consumer choices influence what companies produce
Individual habits add up across millions of people
Governments respond to public pressure
examples: Plastic bag charges cut bag use sharply in several countries
Consumer demand has pushed carmakers towards electric models

question: Is working from home a positive trend?
for: No time or money spent commuting
More flexibility for family responsibilities
Fewer cars on the road at peak times
against: Harder for junior staff to learn
Isolation and blurred boundaries between work and home
City-centre businesses lose customers
examples: Many firms now use hybrid working, with two or three office days a week

question: Should unhealthy food be taxed?
for: Higher prices reduce consumption
Money raised can fund healthcare or sport
Encourages companies to make healthier products
against: Hits poorer families hardest
People may simply buy cheaper unhealthy food
Education may be more effective than price
examples: Sugar taxes have led some drinks makers to reduce sugar in their products

question: Should cars be banned from city centres?
for: Cleaner air and less noise
Safer streets for pedestrians and cyclists
More space for parks and cafés
against: Difficult for disabled and elderly people
Businesses may lose customers who drive
Public transport must be good enough first
examples: Several European city centres have become pedestrian zones
Congestion charges are a middle option

question: Should young people care for elderly parents at home?
for: Strong family bonds and respect for elders
Elderly people often prefer to stay at home
Cheaper than professional care
against: Carers may have to give up work
Some people need specialist medical care
Small modern homes may not have space
examples: In many cultures, several generations traditionally live together

question: Is news on social media reliable?
for: News spreads quickly in emergencies
People can see eyewitness reports
More voices are heard than in traditional media
against: False stories spread faster than corrections
Algorithms show people only views they already hold
Little checking of facts
examples: Fact-checking organisations now work with some platforms

question: Does tourism do more good than harm?
for: Creates jobs and brings money to local economies
Encourages protection of heritage sites
Promotes understanding between cultures
against: Overcrowding damages popular sites
Housing becomes holiday rentals and prices rise
Profits often go to foreign companies
examples: Some cities limit cruise ships or charge visitor fees

question: Should governments fund the arts?
for: Art reflects and preserves national identity
Free museums make culture available to everyone
The arts support tourism and creative industries
against: Money may be needed more for health and education
Popular art can fund itself through ticket sales
Officials should not decide which art is worthwhile
examples: Free entry to national museums has increased visitor numbers in some countries

question: Are professional athletes paid too much?
for: Their pay is far higher than that of nurses or teachers
Careers depend on luck as well as effort
High salaries make ticket prices rise
against: Careers are short and risky
They generate huge income for clubs and sponsors
Salaries reflect market demand
examples: Many athletes retire before the age of thirty-five

question: Should schools teach practical life skills?
for: Students need to manage money and cook
Many young people leave school unprepared for adult life
Practical skills can motivate students who struggle with academic subjects
against: The school day is already full
Parents can teach these skills at home
Academic subjects build knowledge that is hard to learn elsewhere
examples: Some schools include personal finance lessons in maths classes

question: Will artificial intelligence take people's jobs?
for: Routine office and factory tasks can be automated
Companies can cut costs by using software
Change may be faster than workers can retrain
against: New technologies have always created new kinds of jobs
AI can make workers more productive rather than replace them
Many jobs need human judgement and care
examples: Bank tellers became fewer after cash machines, but banks opened more branches for a time

question: Should money be spent on protecting wild animals?
for: Biodiversity supports food production and medicine
Once a species is lost, it cannot be recovered
Wildlife tourism brings income to poorer regions
against: Human needs such as healthcare are more urgent
Some projects are expensive with little success
Money may be better spent on reducing pollution
examples: Protected reserves have helped some endangered species recover
